case_study_insert.main_stem: Vireo Managed IT Services (VMS) is a private limited company in the managed IT services sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2014 by Elena Petrova, the business provides outsourced helpdesk, network monitoring and cybersecurity support to small and medium enterprises and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. VMS plans to invest $980,000 in a new security operations centre targeting healthcare clients, financed by $600,000 of venture capital and $380,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $26.50 a unit and a selling price of $36.50, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. VMS faces a serious people problem: remote-work communication breakdowns between field engineers and the office dropped client response times and drove complaint volumes up across three regions.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — September 2026: The service desk closed 3,860 tickets last quarter with an average resolution time of 5.6 hours and a first-time fix rate of 78%. Client uptime SLA compliance was 99.1% across 640 monitored devices. A third-party audit found 4 critical vulnerabilities, down from 9 six months ago. 31 of 64 staff hold security certifications; off-the-job SOC certification at the cyber college costs $2,000 per engineer. 28 named hospital trusts have already requested proposals for the healthcare security operations centre.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Vireo Managed IT Services for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Business Technology Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, the third rise this year, lifting borrowing costs for IT services firms. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $11.80 to $12.53 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for junior field technicians. (3) Cyber-insurance premiums rose 14.8% year-on-year, technology input costs rose 6.9%, and SME spending on outsourced IT grew 8.6% in the same period.

questions.question_text: VMS plans to finance its $980,000 security operations centre with $600,000 of venture capital. Explain two advantages for VMS of using venture capital instead of relying only on retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Venture capital provides the $600,000 VMS needs without draining the $380,000 retained profit, which remains available to fund working capital, 64 salaries and the three regional teams while complaint volumes are worked through. Retained profit of $380,000 alone would leave almost nothing for a $980,000 build, so external capital lets the healthcare security operations centre proceed now rather than after years of accumulation.

Point 2: Venture capital investors typically add more than cash — sector contacts, governance and credibility with large hospital trusts. That expertise directly supports the healthcare launch, because 28 named hospital trusts have already requested proposals and a respected backer reassures procurement boards. Unlike a bank loan, venture capital carries no fixed monthly repayments, protecting VMS's cash flow and the 99.1% SLA service at a time when the base interest rate has risen to 5.75% and borrowing is expensive. For a business whose interest payable already climbed from $22,000 in 2024 to $40,000 in 2025, avoiding fresh debt service preserves room for the certified-staff costs the healthcare launch will demand.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Vireo Managed IT Services and its healthcare expansion.

questions.question_text: VMS is launching its healthcare security operations centre. Consider healthcare-IT trade-conference exhibitions, direct mail to hospital chief information officers, or a targeted webinar series for hospital IT leaders. Which should VMS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Healthcare-IT trade-conference exhibitions: Exhibiting puts VMS in front of hospital IT leaders with live demonstrations of its monitoring capability — 640 monitored devices at 99.1% SLA uptime is a persuasive story on a stand. However, conferences are episodic, geographically concentrated and expensive once travel, stand fees and senior engineer time are included, and a 64-person firm cannot be everywhere its buyers gather.

Direct mail to hospital CIOs: Targeted letters and brochures reach named decision-makers cheaply, and the 28 named hospital trusts on the enquiries list already expect contact. But print direct mail has low response rates, is easy to discard as junk, cannot demonstrate live monitoring, and feels outdated to cybersecurity buyers who expect digital proof.

Targeted webinar series for hospital IT leaders: Webinars let VMS demonstrate real incident-response performance to hundreds of CIOs nationwide at low cost, with instant Q&A, recorded replays and measurable registration data. They suit a considered B2B sale where trust and technical credibility decide contracts, and each session can reference the 4 critical vulnerabilities found by the third-party audit to make the threat concrete.

Recommendation: VMS should choose the targeted webinar series. It reaches the entire national healthcare buyer pool, is cheap and measurable, and showcases exactly the security operations centre capability the 28 interested trusts want to assess. Conference exhibitions are rejected as too infrequent and regional to sustain a national launch on their own, and direct mail is rejected as a low-impact channel that cannot prove 99.1% SLA delivery — one or two flagship conferences can be layered on later once the webinar pipeline converts prospects into proposals.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VMS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of VMS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why conferences and direct mail are rejected.

questions.question_text: VMS faces remote-work communication breakdowns that dropped client response times and drove complaints up across three regions. Explain two benefits for VMS of using autocratic leadership in its incident-response team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership gives the incident-response team one clear decision-maker during critical outages, so diagnosis, client communication and fixes happen fast and consistently — vital when the average resolution time is already 5.6 hours and clients expect 99.1% uptime SLA compliance. A single authoritative voice prevents the confusion and duplicated effort that remote-work communication breakdowns have caused, cutting response times and complaint volumes across the three affected regions.

Point 2: Clear rules, fixed escalation paths and strict accountability suit a hierarchical structure with safety-critical work: junior engineers know exactly who approves containment steps, which reduces errors on the 4 critical vulnerabilities identified by the audit. Autocratic discipline also makes training and onboarding quicker for field engineers, supports standardised runbooks across regions, and frees senior staff to pursue the healthcare expansion rather than mediating disputes — reinforcing the orderly roll-out of the new security operations centre to 28 interested hospital trusts.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VMS's complaints, resolution times, SLA and expansion.

questions.question_text: VMS must staff the new healthcare security operations centre. Consider external recruitment of experienced security analysts or off-the-job SOC certification of its own engineers at $2,000 per employee. Which should VMS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
External recruitment of experienced analysts: Hiring certified analysts delivers immediate capability for the healthcare launch — hospital trusts expect day-one competence, and the 28 interested trusts will audit the team before signing. External hires bring exposure to other hospital networks, instant credibility in proposals, and no training lag. However, experienced analysts command high salaries and signing bonuses, compete in a scarce market, and may leave within a year; onboarding costs and culture fit with VMS's hierarchical, autocratic style are real risks, and salary inflation would raise fixed costs above $300,000 a year permanently.

Off-the-job SOC certification of existing engineers: The cyber college course at $2,000 per engineer gives structured, recognised skills for 16 chosen engineers at a total of $32,000 — trivial against the $980,000 build. Existing staff already understand VMS's clients, tools and 99.1% SLA commitments, morale rises when staff see investment in their careers, and retention improves because seconded engineers return to a clear promotion path. Drawbacks: certification takes weeks, projects pause while staff study, and success depends on engineers' aptitude — some may not reach the required standard.

Decision: VMS should choose off-the-job SOC certification for its own engineers, plus one external senior hire as SOC lead. Training at $2,000 per head is far cheaper than market salaries, builds loyalty, and turns the remote-work communication problem into an opportunity by training regional pods together. Blanket external recruitment is rejected: locking the business into premium salaries and an unproven, disconnected team would strain the venture-capital funding plan and undermine the healthcare launch's credibility with hospital trusts that value stable, certified incumbents.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two staffing options with limited application to VMS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of VMS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of VMS with a well-justified decision covering cost, speed, retention and healthcare-client expectations.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VMS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($36.50 − $26.50) = $300,000 ÷ $10.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $36.50 − $26.50 = $10.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $10.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VMS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 40,000 units to confirm a margin of safety of 10,000 units, informing whether the new healthcare security operations centre can reach profitability within its venture-capital plan.
2. Contribution per unit of $10.00 lets managers price multi-year hospital contracts, modelling for example a 4% volume discount to $35.04, which would still leave $8.54 contribution and about 35,129 units needed to cover fixed costs, letting VMS judge the deal before signing.
3. Knowing the break-even point helps managers set monthly service-contract targets for the sales pipeline of 28 named hospital trusts, checking cumulative signed units stay comfortably above 30,000 before further venture capital is requested.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($300,000 ÷ 40,000 units + $26.50 = $34.00 a unit) to benchmark each region, identify the rework driving client complaints and the 78% first-time fix rate, and renegotiate vendor input costs amid the 6.9% technology input-cost rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $10.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 10,000 units versus 40,000-unit output; contract pricing against $300,000 fixed costs; pipeline targets for 28 hospital trusts; and unit-cost benchmarking at $34.00 to cut complaints and input-cost pressure.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VMS's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has VMS's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 42.4%
Profit Margin 2024 = 16.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 20.0%
ROCE 2024 = 19.5%
ROCE 2025 = 24.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 — revenue $2,150,000 − cost of sales $1,290,000 = gross profit $860,000; 860 ÷ 2,150 × 100 = 40.0%. Operating profit $344,000 ÷ revenue $2,150,000 × 100 = 16.0%. Operating profit ÷ capital employed $1,760,000 × 100 = 19.5%. 2025 — revenue $2,640,000 − cost of sales $1,520,000 = gross profit $1,120,000; 1,120 ÷ 2,640 × 100 = 42.4%. Operating profit $528,000 ÷ revenue $2,640,000 × 100 = 20.0%. Operating profit ÷ capital employed $2,200,000 × 100 = 24.0%.

Evaluation: Profitability has strengthened across the board. Direct costs grew more slowly than revenue, widening the gross gap from 40.0% to 42.4%, and disciplined overheads pushed the bottom-line measure from 16.0% to 20.0% while operating profit rose 53.5% on 22.8% revenue growth. Returns on capital jumped from 19.5% to 24.0% even though capital employed grew 25.0%, showing the healthcare-focused investment is already generating returns. Cautions: interest payable rose from $22,000 to $40,000 as venture capital and credit tightened, and the 2025 figures assume the 28 hospital trust proposals convert; if healthcare contracts slip, utilisation of the new security operations centre will disappoint and the ratios could deteriorate quickly.

Conclusion: VMS's profitability has improved. All three measures rose (40.0% to 42.4%, 16.0% to 20.0%, 19.5% to 24.0%), growth came from margin gains and efficient capital use rather than leverage, and the cost base was controlled well. VMS should lock in multi-year hospital contracts and keep the certified team stable to defend these ratios through the launch year.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit, interest and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether VMS's profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VMS of switching ticket closure from a final quality-control inspection to built-in quality assurance checks.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Built-in quality assurance prevents errors before tickets close instead of catching them afterwards, raising the 78% first-time fix rate and protecting the 99.1% SLA compliance that justifies premium pricing on 640 monitored devices. Fewer reopened tickets mean less rework, lower labour cost per fix and happier clients, reducing the complaint volumes that have climbed across three regions since the remote-work communication breakdowns began — and supporting the credibility needed to sign the 28 interested hospital trusts, who increasingly demand prevention-based assurance evidence rather than after-the-fact inspection.

Disadvantage: Quality assurance requires up-front checklist design, engineer training and ongoing peer review, which costs time that a 64-person team already stretched by 3,860 tickets a quarter can scarcely spare. Closure times may lengthen initially, and weak or inconsistent checklists can become box-ticking exercises that add bureaucracy without stopping defects — particularly risky where the audit already found 4 critical vulnerabilities and clients expect every fix verified before sign-off.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VMS's tickets, SLA, complaints and healthcare launch.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 14.8% rise in cyber-insurance premiums will affect VMS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): VMS is venture-capital funded with minimal long-term debt, so the immediate cash effect is small — mainly costlier overdrafts and future asset finance for the security operations centre. The bigger risk is indirect: pricier borrowing cools SME appetite for big outsourced-IT projects, although Appendix 3 notes SME spending on outsourced IT still grew 8.6%, which softens the blow.

Minimum wage increase (6.2% to $12.53): Many of VMS's junior field technicians and helpdesk staff work near the minimum wage — roughly 30 of the 64 employees. An annual wage bill near $780,000 for that group rises by about $48,000 from April 2026. Because VMS sells fixed-price monitoring and support contracts, the increase cannot be passed through instantly, squeezing the $10.00 contribution per unit on the $26.50 variable cost; it also fuels pay-compression demands from team leaders just below the new floor.

Cyber-insurance premium rise (14.8%): MSSP cover is already expensive; if VMS pays roughly $120,000 a year in premiums, a 14.8% rise adds about $17,800. Premiums can be shared in client contract pricing and demand for certified managed detection is rising, so this cost is partly recoverable and signals a market growing 8.6% this year — a genuine tailwind wrapped around a cost.

Conclusion: The 6.2% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It is recurring, hits the largest block of payroll headcount directly, lands on fixed-price contracts where pass-through is slow, and lands exactly when the remote-work communication rebuild already strains capacity. The insurance rise is second and partly recoverable through pricing, while the interest rate increase is the smallest near-term effect for a VC-backed firm with low debt — VMS should respond with scheduling automation, productivity targets and selective price reviews at renewal.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to VMS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VMS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VMS with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
